prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture without specific clinical indication for CNS infection or encephalitis.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not manage the postictal dysphasia as a stroke: it followed a witnessed seizure, resolved within minutes, and the MRI shows no restricted diffusion.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for efficacy and tolerability; neither interacts with loratadine.

Give seizure safety advice (showers rather than baths, no swimming alone, no work at heights) and advise regular sleep and limited alcohol.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism, no immunosuppression and recovering as expected after the seizure: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.

Epigastric and deja vu aura, automatisms, dystonic posturing and postictal dysphasia make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

No headache; migraine aura does not produce behavioral arrest with automatisms or progress to a tonic-clonic seizure with postictal dysphasia.

key_clinical_evidence: Three to four stereotyped rising epigastric and deja vu auras a month for nine months, two partner-witnessed episodes with impaired awareness and an identical episode three years ago are prior focal seizures, so the two-unprovoked-seizure criterion for epilepsy is met [ILAE_def_2014].

Right-hand dystonic posturing is contralateral to the onset and postictal dysphasia points to the language-dominant hemisphere, while left-hand automatisms are usually ipsilateral; all point to the left, concordant with left hippocampal sclerosis on MRI and left anterior temporal discharges on EEG [Lateralization_2005].
A febrile seizure in infancy is a recognized antecedent of hippocampal sclerosis.
First-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy is lamotrigine or levetiracetam [NICE_NG217_2025]; lamotrigine was more effective than levetiracetam in SANAD II [SANAD2_2021].

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Novak is a 33-year-old right-handed graphic designer who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His partner reports that approximately four hours prior to arrival, the patient suddenly stopped mid-sentence, stared blankly, and began performing repetitive lip-smacking and chewing movements. His right hand assumed a stiff, bent-wrist posture that the partner describes as resembling a clenched fist held up and twisted inward. He did not respond when called. After approximately 20 to 25 seconds, his entire body stiffened and he fell from the couch onto the floor, developing rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting roughly 90 seconds. He was incontinent of urine. Emergency medical services were called. Following the convulsion, the patient was unable to produce coherent speech for approximately five minutes, using jumbled words, before gradually recovering fluency. He was confused and drowsy for a further 25 minutes.

On interview, the patient recalls experiencing an intense wave of nausea rising from his epigastrium toward his throat, immediately followed by an overwhelming and distressing feeling of deja vu, just before losing awareness. He reports having had strikingly similar brief episodes of the rising stomach sensation and deja vu, each lasting 30 to 60 seconds, approximately three to four times per month over the past nine months. He never progressed to convulsive activity during these previous events and remained able to function afterward, though he felt briefly confused and worn out. He discussed one of these episodes with a colleague who suggested it sounded like a panic attack from work stress; an earlier, identical episode while walking to a coffee shop three years ago, the first he remembers, had been attributed by the patient himself to low blood sugar and was not reported to any physician.

On two occasions in the last two months, his partner witnessed him stare blankly, smack his lips, and reach at his shirt with his left hand for roughly half a minute, during which he did not respond. He denies prior convulsions aside from the febrile seizure in infancy. There is no recent head trauma, fever, or illness. No prior antiepileptic medications. Sleep has been normal.

Partner reports the patient was unable to speak coherently for approximately five minutes following the convulsion, speaking in short, jumbled phrases before recovering full fluency.
